title: Steam Turbine

introduction.definition: A steam turbine converts the thermal energy of steam into rotation. Stationary nozzles accelerate the steam, and moving blades on the rotor turn its velocity into torque, stage after stage, while the steam expands to the exhaust (condenser) pressure. A governor valve controls the steam flow to hold speed or load.
applications: Power generation (thermal, nuclear, solar thermal, biomass)
key_points: Many stages; blades grow longer toward the exhaust

classification.type: Multistage, condensing, single casing, impulse/reaction stages

introduction.summary: A steam turbine converts the energy of high-pressure steam into shaft power. In each stage, stationary nozzles accelerate the steam and the moving blades on the rotor turn that velocity into torque. The steam expands through many stages to the condenser vacuum, so the blades get longer toward the exhaust. A governor valve controls the steam flow to hold speed or load.

working_principle.characteristic_curve: Willans line: steam flow vs power is nearly linear; efficiency depends on stage design and exhaust vacuum.

pressure.title: Steam pressure through the stages
pressure.description: Steam expands stage by stage: in each nozzle row pressure falls and velocity rises; the moving blades turn that velocity into torque. Volume grows as pressure falls, so blades get longer toward the exhaust (condenser vacuum).

foundation: Table-top concrete or steel foundation with dynamic analysis; turbine–generator alignment includes catenary.
alignment: Align driver and driven shafts with a laser or dial-indicator method to the coupling maker's tolerances; re-check hot alignment where thermal growth is significant.
piping: Steam lines drained and warmed before admission; limit piping forces on casing nozzles (NEMA SM 23 / API 612).
commissioning: Check rotation direction with the coupling disconnected.
Fill lubricant to the correct level and grade.
Start unloaded where possible; record vibration, temperatures, current and pressures as a baseline.

overhaul.task: Open casing: inspect blades, diaphragms, seals; clean deposits.

lubrication: Forced lube-oil system for journal and thrust bearings; control oil for governor.

video_tutorials.title: Steam Turbine — Introduction

script.narration: This module introduces the Steam Turbine.
A steam turbine converts the thermal energy of steam into rotation.
Stationary nozzles accelerate the steam, and moving blades on the rotor turn its velocity into torque, stage after stage, while the steam expands to the exhaust (condenser) pressure.
A governor valve controls the steam flow to hold speed or load.
Typical applications include power generation (thermal, nuclear, solar thermal, biomass); driving compressors and pumps (mechanical drive); cogeneration (back-pressure/extraction); marine propulsion.
The cutaway reveals the internal construction: Turbine Casing (Inlet End, Exhaust Hood) & Steam Chest, Rotor: Shaft, Wheels (Discs) & Moving Blades (6 stages).
The exploded view separates every component so each one can be tapped for its function, material and failure modes.
Next, watch the operation tutorial to see how it works.

video_tutorials.title: Steam Turbine — Operation

script.narration: How the Steam Turbine works.
High-pressure steam enters through the steam chest and governor (control) valve.
Fixed nozzles in each diaphragm accelerate the steam.
The steam jet pushes the moving blades and turns the rotor.
Stage by stage the pressure falls and the volume grows — blades get longer.
Exhaust steam goes down to the condenser; the rotor drives the generator through the coupling.
The flow overlay traces the liquid from suction to discharge.
Steam expands stage by stage: in each nozzle row pressure falls and velocity rises; the moving blades turn that velocity into torque.

video_tutorials.title: Steam Turbine — Maintenance

script.narration: Maintenance essentials for the Steam Turbine.
Monitor vibration, bearing temperatures, expansion, eccentricity.
Overspeed trip test; valve stem free-movement test.
Lube-oil analysis.
Open casing: inspect blades, diaphragms, seals; clean deposits.
Watch for blade erosion / fouling: efficiency loss. Common cause: wet steam, carry-over of silica/salts.
Watch for high vibration: trip on vibration. Common cause: rub, imbalance, misalignment, bowed rotor.
Watch for sticking control valve: poor speed control. Common cause: deposits on stem.
Record every inspection so trends — vibration, temperature, leakage and performance — can be compared over time.
